question: Is awakening reached by one's own practice (self-power) or by the power of Amitābha's vow (other-power)?

sides.position: Awakening is to see one's own nature; the Pure Land is in the purified mind and Amitābha is one's own nature; seeking a Buddha outside is delusion (as the Pure Land texts report the objection).
arguments: The Platform Sūtra asks where the man of the West will seek birth if he does evil.

sides.position: In an age without a buddha one cannot reach non-retrogression by self-power; the easy path is to be born by riding the power of the vow; Amitābha's vow is the dominant condition.
arguments: Nāgārjuna's water route; the lame man on another's ship; the three vows that prove other-power.

sides.position: Birth is by other-power through the nenbutsu that accords with the vow; one keeps calling all one's life.
Nothing is self-power: shinjin and the nenbutsu are given; the self-power good person is not the object of the vow until he turns; self-power nenbutsu leads only to the transformed land.

historical_debates.name: Ōhara dialogue
historical_debates.accounts: Hōnen before Tendai and Nara scholars at Shōrin-in, Ōhara (Hōnen biographies).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Jōdo-shū: the scholars were moved and joined the nenbutsu.

reconciliation.explanation: The Pure Land tradition itself presents the holy path and the Pure Land as two gates suited to different capacities and ages (Daochuo), a reconciliation by temperament and stage of the student.
reconciliation.detail: Chinese masters (Yanshou, Zhuhong) accept both gates and even join them; Hōnen sets the holy path aside for himself and his age without denying its truth.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Shinshū denies that self-power can bring birth in the true land and would not accept that the two are equal paths; Chan teachers who reject seeking outside would not accept the Western land as more than expedient.

question: Is the Pure Land a real land in the West, or the purified mind only?

sides.position: The Western land is to be sought really; birth there is the 'birth of non-birth'; mind-only and the Western land are not two, and those whose power is not sufficient must be born there.
arguments: Only those who can live in a latrine without disgust may say every place is the West (Zhuhong).
The wise seek birth ardently while knowing its nature cannot be found (Shiyi lun).

sides.position: The Pure Land is the pure mind; 'as the mind is pure the buddha-land is pure'; Amitābha is one's own nature (as reported by Pure Land writers answering the view).
The Pure Land is pointed to in a direction and given form (Shandao) for ordinary beings; it is a reward land, not merely mind.
The Buddha seen in the samādhi neither comes nor goes; mind makes the buddha (Pratyutpanna; Contemplation Sūtra 8).

historical_debates.name: Huiyuan's question to Kumārajīva
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Kumārajīva: the vision is not false; seen by the Buddha's power, the samādhi and one's merit.

reconciliation.explanation: Chinese Pure Land masters reconcile mind-only (ultimate level) with the Western land (conventional level, a skilful means for those of insufficient power) — a reconciliation made within the tradition.
reconciliation.detail: Tanluan's birth of non-birth, the Jingtu shiyi lun's appeal to the two truths, Yanshou and Zhuhong.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Jōdo-shū and Shinshū reject dissolving the Western land into mind; Chan radicals reject the need for any land.

question: Is birth settled by one calling (or one thought of faith), or by lifelong many callings?

sides.position: (Kōsai, ichinengi) Birth is settled in a single thought of faith / one calling; further callings add nothing.
(Ryūkan, tanengi) One should call continuously all one's life, as Shandao taught ('until the end of life').
Neither should be insisted on; the nenbutsu of the primal vow includes both; one thought-moment of shinjin settles birth and the callings follow in gratitude.

historical_debates.name: One-calling / many-calling controversy in Hōnen's circle
historical_debates.accounts: Hōnen's letters; Ryūkan's tract; Shinran's Ichinen tanen mon'i.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Hōnen warned against the excesses of one-calling; Shinran counselled against insisting on either.

reconciliation.explanation: Hōnen: believe with one calling (standpoint of faith), practise with many (standpoint of practice); Shinran: do not set one against the other.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The historical ichinengi and tanengi parties each held the other in error; their lines did not survive.

question: Can those who have committed the five grave offences or slandered the Dharma be born in the Pure Land?

sides.position: The eighteenth vow excludes those who commit the five grave offences and slander the true Dharma (the Sanskrit likewise).
The Contemplation Sūtra's lowest grade: one who has committed the five offences and ten evils is born by ten recitations at death.
(Tanluan) One guilty of both offences and slander cannot be born; one who committed the offences without slandering can, since slander rejects the very Dharma.
(Shandao) The vow's exclusion is a gate of restraint to deter; once committed, these too are embraced.
(Shinran) Even the 'difficult to cure' — slanderers, grave offenders, icchantikas — are healed, as Ajātaśatru was.

reconciliation.explanation: Shandao reads the exclusion as a skilful deterrent (gate of restraint) and the lower-grade birth as the gate of embrace — the tradition's own reconciliation by skilful means.
reconciliation.detail: Tanluan's earlier solution (distinguishing slander) is retained as a reading of degree.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Tanluan's position that slanderers cannot be born is not the same as Shandao's; the two readings are recorded side by side.

question: Is Amitābha a reward-body buddha in a reward land, or a transformation body in a land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together?

sides.position: (Jingying Huiyuan and other Sui scholars, as reported) Sukhāvatī is a land manifested for beings; the upper grades are sages of the stages; ordinary beings are born into a lower land.
(Daochuo, Shandao) Amitābha is a reward buddha and Sukhāvatī a reward land; the old view is 'a great error'; ordinary beings enter by the vow's power; all nine grades are ordinary beings.
(Tiantai four-land scheme, as later Pure Land writers use it) Sukhāvatī is chiefly the land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, while also containing the higher lands.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the two sides classify the same land within different three-body/four-land schemes.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: 'reward' from the Buddha's side (fruit of the vow), 'land shared by ordinary beings' from the beings' side
P4-stage: the land appears according to the capacity of those born (Tiantai four lands)

notes: The Sui opponents' view is recorded as reported by Shandao and Daochuo (reported_by_opponent).

question: Does the promise of birth by vows or ten recitations bring birth at once, or only at 'another time' (Mahāyānasaṃgraha)?

sides.position: (Mahāyānasaṃgraha teachers, as reported) Sayings that one is born by merely vowing are an 'intention for another time': they create a cause that ripens only in a distant future, as one coin buys a thousand only in time.

(Daochuo) A treatise cannot contradict the sūtra; the ten-recitation reciter has hidden past causes and is born at once. (Huaigan) 'By vow alone' means a bare vow without practice; sincere recitation is practice of body, speech and mind, so birth follows at once.

historical_debates.name: The bieshiyi controversy
historical_debates.accounts: Anle ji; Shi jingtu qunyi lun; Shandao's commentary.

reconciliation.explanation: Huaigan's distinction: the 'another time' statement concerns a bare vow (provisional encouragement), while calling the name with the three acts is practice that brings birth — the two refer to different cases.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Yogācāra side's own later response is not recorded here.

notes: The Mahāyānasaṃgraha side is known here only as reported by Pure Land authors.

question: Should one aspire to Maitreya's Tuṣita or to Amitābha's Sukhāvatī?

sides.position: (Aspirants to Tuṣita, as reported) Maitreya is the next buddha; being born in Tuṣita one hears him and descends with him; the ten goods suffice.
Tuṣita is in the desire realm, a place of retrogression and sensual attachment, without a vow to receive beings; in Sukhāvatī all are non-retrogressive and the vow and light embrace reciters.

historical_debates.name: Tuṣita vs Sukhāvatī comparisons
historical_debates.accounts: Anle ji; Jingtu shiyi lun; Xifang yaojue.

reconciliation.explanation: Both are Mahāyāna aspirations to be near a buddha; the Pure Land texts rank them by ease and non-retrogression rather than denying Tuṣita's value.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Daochuo and the Shiyi lun insist that the difference is 'great in substance', not merely of temperament.

notes: Xuanzang and Kuiji personally aspired to Tuṣita (recalled); the Xifang yaojue attributed to Kuiji nonetheless favours the West.

question: Is the aspiration for awakening (bodhicitta) required for birth in the Pure Land?

sides.position: (Tanluan; the Larger Sūtra's three grades; the three meritorious acts) All aspirants must arouse bodhicitta, which is the vow to save beings; seeking birth for pleasure does not bring birth.
(Hōnen) Bodhicitta is among the practices mentioned for the three grades in order to be set aside in favour of the nenbutsu alone.
(Myōe) Discarding bodhicitta is the first great error of the Senchakushū; without it the nenbutsu is not Buddhism.
(Shinran) The true bodhicitta is other-power: shinjin itself, given by Amida.

historical_debates.name: Myōe's Zaijarin against the Senchakushū
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Jōdo and Shinshū answered through later commentaries and Shinran's other-power bodhicitta.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the sides disagree whether bodhicitta is a practitioner's condition or is subsumed in (or given with) the nenbutsu.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Shinran relocates bodhicitta to the Buddha's side, where Myōe's requirement and Hōnen's selection might both hold
P4-stage: bodhicitta as required for higher grades only (Senchakushū's parallel reading)

question: May the nenbutsu be practised exclusively, setting aside all other practices and deities?

sides.position: Yes: the primal vow selected the nenbutsu alone; set aside the holy path, the miscellaneous practices and the auxiliary acts.

(Kōfukuji, Jōkei) No: exclusive nenbutsu slights Śākyamuni and the kami, hinders all good practices, misunderstands the nenbutsu as mere calling, harms the order and disturbs the nation (nine errors).
(Myōe) The Senchakushū discards bodhicitta and calls holy-path practitioners bandits.
(Nichiren) The nenbutsu leads to the Avīci hell; the Senchakushū's 'set aside' is slander of the Lotus (Risshō ankoku ron).
(Shinran) The persecution was contrary to the Dharma; he became neither monk nor layman.

historical_debates.name: Jōgen persecution
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Four disciples executed; Hōnen, Shinran and others laicised and exiled.

historical_debates.name: Karoku persecution
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Blocks of the Senchakushū burned; Ryūkan and others exiled (recalled).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: an exclusivist claim about the one practice for this age against the view that exclusivity denies the other teachings.
candidate_readings: P3-path: exclusive nenbutsu as one temperament's path, all others valid for others (Hōnen's own Seven-Article Pledge forbids disparaging other schools)
P4-stage / age: selection as fitted to the last age (Daochuo's time and capacity)

question: Is birth settled only at death with the Buddha's welcome, or already in this life?

sides.position: Right mindfulness at death and Amida's welcoming descent are sought; the nenbutsu is continued so that the practitioner is welcomed.
Deathbed rites and assisted recitation secure right mindfulness; Daochuo's wax seal: the moment life ends is the moment of birth.
The welcome belongs to those of various practices; the person of shinjin is settled at the moment of shinjin and need not wait for the moment of death.

reconciliation.explanation: Shinran himself assigns the welcome at death to practitioners of the nineteenth vow and settlement in life to those of the eighteenth — a distinction by the practitioner's stage.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Jōdo-shū does not accept that its practitioners are of the nineteenth vow.

question: Is the cause of birth the nenbutsu (with the three minds) or shinjin?

sides.position: The nenbutsu is the rightly determined act and cause of birth; the three minds accompany it.
Shinjin is the true cause (shinjin shōin); the nenbutsu is the expression of gratitude (shōmyō hōon).

historical_debates.name: The debate on shinjin in Hōnen's circle
historical_debates.accounts: Godenshō (the 'debate on shinjin' episode, Shinran's claim that his shinjin and Hōnen's were one)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Shinshū: Hōnen affirmed that shinjin, being given by the Buddha, is the same in all.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled between the schools.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: from the practice side the nenbutsu, from the entrusting side shinjin — Hōnen's 'believe with one calling, practise with the whole life'
Shinran's own claim that the name and shinjin are inseparable (the name as the cause, shinjin as the condition, or the reverse)

question: Should Chan meditation and Pure Land recitation be practised together?

sides.position: Yes: both return to the one source; Chan is the Chan of Pure Land and Pure Land the Pure Land of Chan; practise one gate deeply; all good practices share one end.
Mixing practices loses birth; exclusive practice alone is right.
Recitation is for those of lesser capacity, or a huatou; seeking a Buddha outside is contrary to seeing one's nature (as reported).

reconciliation.explanation: Zhuhong's 'return to the source is not two, expedient gates are many' reconciles by path, while urging depth in one gate.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Shandao's line (and Jōdo-shū) warns that mixed practice fails; Chan purists deny the need.

question: Can practices other than the nenbutsu bring birth in the Pure Land?

sides.position: Yes: the three meritorious acts, the sixteen contemplations and all good roots dedicated to birth lead there (the sūtras; Chinese masters).

(Hōnen) They are set aside; the primal vow's practice is the nenbutsu alone. (Chōsai, as reported) The various practices too are vowed in the primal vow. (Benchō's line, as usually stated) They can bring birth but are not the vow's own practice.
They lead only to the transformed land (19th vow).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled among Hōnen's disciples' lines.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: other practices for those unable to entrust exclusively (Shinran's provisional gate)
P6-upaya: other practices taught to lead beings toward the nenbutsu (Senchakushū 4's first reading)

notes: Positions of Chōsai and Benchō given in general terms only (low confidence).

question: Must one petition Amida with body, speech and mind (sangō kimyō) to be saved?

sides.position: (The Honganji academy's heads, as usually reported) One should rely on Amida with the three acts — bowing, calling for help and wishing — as the form of entrusting.
(Their provincial critics) Entrusting is the one thought of shinjin given by Amida; requiring the three acts is self-power.

historical_debates.name: Sangō wakuran
historical_debates.accounts: Nishi Honganji controversy settled by the shogunate's intervention (recalled).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: The three-acts view was judged erroneous (recalled).

reconciliation.explanation: Recorded as a historical controversy; not reconciled here.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: three acts as the outward form of shinjin vs as its condition

notes: Participants' names not recalled with confidence and omitted; to be sourced.
